question: What is the main job of hormones in our bodies?

options.A: Generate rapid electrical impulses for muscle contraction
options.B: Transport oxygen molecules from the lungs to body tissues
options.C: Filter waste products directly out of the bloodstream
options.D: Act as chemical messengers to regulate target organs

explanation: Think of hormones as chemical text messages sent through the blood to tell different organs what to do. You've got this! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T4#GNS211_U1_T4_h1)

question: How is endocrine signaling different from nervous system signaling?

options.A: Nervous signaling produces much slower, permanent bodily changes
options.B: Nervous signaling relies entirely on circulating blood vessels
options.C: Endocrine signaling uses direct physical contact with cells
options.D: Endocrine signaling is slower and has longer-lasting effects

explanation: Nerve impulses are like a quick flash of lightning, while hormones are like a slow, steady wave whose effects linger much longer. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T4#GNS211_U1_T4_h1)

question: Which part of the brain connects the nervous system to the endocrine system?
explanation: The hypothalamus is the master bridge! It takes messages from the brain and turns them into hormonal orders. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T4#GNS211_U1_T4_h2)

question: What is the main job of the posterior pituitary gland?

options.A: It breaks down worn-out hormones in the bloodstream
options.B: It stores and releases hormones produced by the hypothalamus
options.C: It manufactures tropic hormones for the adrenal glands
options.D: It controls blood calcium levels using direct neural input

explanation: The posterior pituitary acts like a warehouse—it doesn't make hormones itself, but safely stores and releases them when needed. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T4#GNS211_U1_T4_h2)

question: What triggers hormone release during humoral stimulation?

options.A: Tropic hormones secreted by the anterior pituitary
options.B: Emotional stress and physical trauma responses
options.C: Changes in ion or nutrient levels in the blood
options.D: Direct electrical impulses sent from the brain

explanation: Humoral stimuli mean the glands are tasting the blood directly—like checking if there is too much sugar or calcium floating around. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T4#GNS211_U1_T4_h3)

question: A patient just ate a heavy meal loaded with carbs. What happens right away?

options.A: The parathyroid will secrete parathyroid hormone due to calcium shifts
options.B: The adrenal cortex will stop producing cortisol entirely
options.C: The pancreas will release insulin due to rising blood glucose
options.D: The hypothalamus will block all tropic hormone production

explanation: As sugar rises in the blood after eating, the pancreas senses it directly and releases insulin to bring it back down. Simple and smart! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T4#GNS211_U1_T4_h3)

question: Which gland gets a direct emergency signal from nerves during stress?
explanation: When you get a sudden fright, the nervous system instantly triggers the adrenal medulla to pump out adrenaline for that fight-or-flight burst. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T4#GNS211_U1_T4_h4)

question: Why is it helpful for the body to use direct nerve control during sudden danger?

options.A: It relies entirely on blood nutrient concentration changes
options.B: It ensures long-term maintenance of blood calcium levels
options.C: It provides a much faster response than hormonal feedback loops
options.D: It prevents the pancreas from secreting too much insulin

explanation: When danger strikes, you don't have time to wait for slow chemical travel—nerves act in a split second to keep you safe! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T4#GNS211_U1_T4_h4)

question: What is the main goal of a negative feedback loop in the body?

options.A: To trigger rapid nerve impulses during acute physical pain
options.B: To maintain hormone levels within a stable, normal range
options.C: To continuously amplify hormone production until exhaustion
options.D: To replace lost nutrients in the extracellular fluid

explanation: Think of negative feedback like an air conditioner: when the room gets too cold (or hormone levels get too high), it turns things off to keep balance. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T4#GNS211_U1_T4_h5)

question: Which of these is a great example of a positive feedback loop?

options.A: Insulin lowering high blood sugar back to normal
options.B: Parathyroid hormone raising low blood calcium levels
options.C: Oxytocin increasing uterine contractions during labor
options.D: Thyroid hormone stopping pituitary TSH production

explanation: Positive feedback pushes a process further and faster until the goal is met, just like oxytocin intensifying contractions until baby arrives! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T4#GNS211_U1_T4_h5)

question: What does 'pulsatile secretion' mean for hormones?

options.A: Stopping all hormone production during nighttime sleep
options.B: Releasing hormones in brief, distinct bursts or pulses
options.C: Secreting hormones at a completely flat, unchanging rate
options.D: Releasing hormones only when blood glucose drops very low

explanation: Instead of pouring out a constant, boring stream, hormones are often released in rhythmic little waves or pulses. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T4#GNS211_U1_T4_h6)

question: Why is it important for the body to release hormones in pulses?

options.A: It ensures constant, unvarying blood pressure all day
options.B: It prevents receptor down-regulation and desensitization
options.C: It stops the nervous system from sending electrical signals
options.D: It triggers immediate humoral stimulation in the pancreas

explanation: If cells are flooded with hormones non-stop, they get 'numb' to them. Pulsing keeps the cell receptors fresh and listening! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T4#GNS211_U1_T4_h6)

question: What medical term describes when a gland makes too little hormone?
explanation: 'Hypo-' means under or low, so hyposecretion simply means the gland is producing less hormone than the body needs. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T4#GNS211_U1_T4_h7)

question: If a patient has a growth causing uncontrolled hypersecretion of a hormone, what happens?

options.A: Complete shutdown of all nervous system reflex pathways
options.B: An exaggerated physiological response and metabolic disturbance
options.C: Permanent cessation of all tropic hormone production
options.D: Immediate reversal of normal circadian rhythm patterns

explanation: 'Hyper-' means too much! Overproducing hormones puts target organs into overdrive, causing clear signs of imbalance. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T4#GNS211_U1_T4_h7)
